states.name: Queensland
general_steps: Check what the council's planning scheme says about your project: some work needs no planning approval, some is code assessable and some is impact assessable.
Talk to the council's planning team before you lodge, especially if the project is unusual. Many councils offer pre-lodgement meetings.

Prepare the application: the state's DA Form 1 (DA Form 2 if it includes building work), owner's consent if you don't own the land, plans, and a report showing how the project meets the planning scheme.
Lodge it with the council and pay the application fee.
Answer any information request from the council by the date it gives.
Impact assessable applications are publicly notified before the council decides.
Building work usually also needs a building approval, normally from a private building certifier.

states.name: New South Wales
general_steps: Check what your council's Local Environmental Plan (LEP) allows on your land. Look up the zone on the NSW Planning Portal Spatial Viewer and order a section 10.7 planning certificate for constraints like heritage, bush fire and flooding.

Check whether your work is exempt development (no approval) or can be complying development (a fast-track CDC from council or a registered certifier) under the State codes. If neither fits, you need a development application (DA).
Talk to your council's duty planner, or book a pre-lodgement meeting, if the project is unusual.

Prepare the DA: plans, a statement of environmental effects, a cost estimate, signed owner's consent, and a BASIX certificate for new homes or work over $50,000. Add any specialist reports, such as a bush fire assessment.
Lodge the DA online on the NSW Planning Portal, then pay the fee when council sends the invoice. The assessment clock starts once you pay.
Council notifies neighbours if needed, may ask for more information, then approves the DA with conditions or refuses it. You can ask for a review or appeal.
Before building, get a construction certificate, appoint a principal certifier and give council at least 2 days' notice. Get an occupation certificate before you move in.

gaps: Planning Portal fees: $43 for a CDC and $47 for other certificates in 2026-27; the portal fee for lodging a DA isn't published.
DA fees here are the maximums in Schedule 4 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Regulation 2021; councils publish their actual fees.

states.name: Victoria
general_steps: Download a free VicPlan planning property report to see your zone, overlays and whether you're in a Bushfire Prone Area.
Read your zone and overlay clauses in your council's planning scheme to see whether a permit is needed. Small second dwellings up to 60 m2 often don't need one.
Check whether your proposal fits a 10 day VicSmart class, and talk to your council's duty planner before you lodge.
Prepare the application: council's planning permit application form, a current copy of title, plans, a written planning report and any specialist reports like a bushfire management statement.
Lodge with your council, usually online, and pay the statutory fee. Council can check it's complete within 5 business days.
Council may ask for more information, refer it to authorities and give notice to neighbours for at least 14 days.
Council decides within 60 statutory days (10 business days for VicSmart). You can ask VCAT to review a refusal or conditions within 60 days.
Then appoint a registered building surveyor for the building permit, and get an occupancy permit before moving in.

source.title: Guide to Victoria's planning system: Planning permits (DTP)

items.label: Certification of a plan of subdivision

gaps: Fees are set by the Planning and Environment (Fees) Regulations 2016 in fee units ($17.27 for 2026-27) and are the same in every council; figures here are from Darebin's published 2026-27 schedule.
There is no single statewide lodgement portal: each council runs its own online lodgement.
Building permits come from a registered building surveyor, with the state levy of 0.128% on work over $10,000 paid to the Building and Plumbing Commission (1300 067 088).
Planning law reforms are commencing in stages until 29 October 2027.

states.name: Western Australia
general_steps: Search your address on PlanWA to find your zone and R-Code, and whether the land is bushfire prone or heritage-listed.

Read your council's local planning scheme and local planning policies. A house or granny flat (up to 70 m2) that meets every R-Codes deemed-to-comply standard is usually exempt from development approval.
Talk to council's duty planner before you lodge, especially if your design varies from the R-Codes.
Prepare the WA application for development approval form, signed by the owner, with plans, a copy of the title and any reports such as a BAL assessment.
Lodge with your council and pay the fee: $147 for work up to $50,000, then 0.32% of the cost up to $500,000.
Council may advertise to neighbours and refer the application to agencies such as the Heritage Council.
Council decides within 60 days, or 90 days if advertised. You can ask the State Administrative Tribunal to review a refusal or conditions.
Then get your building permit (certified, 10 business days, or uncertified, 25 business days) before you start work.
